beats.intro: Lesson four. [[sub]]How to plan ahead of demand, protect quality, and get more from every hour.
beats.order: There are two ways to decide what to make. [[order]]Build to order: wait for the customer, then make it. Safe, but slow. [[wait]]If your sofa takes four months and a competitor delivers in four weeks, you lose the sale. [[fc]]So most businesses build to forecast: they start before the order arrives, betting on demand. [[risk]]The risk is inventory nobody wants. [[hire]]Hiring graduates ahead of need, or building a product for a market you expect, is the same bet.
beats.flows: Building to forecast means running two flows at once. [[make]]One makes the product: raw material, production, finished goods. [[sell]]The other finds the customer: prospect, selling, order. [[dock]]Ideally the product and the order reach the shipping dock at the same moment. [[own]]Ask each team to forecast its own flow, so people answer for their own predictions. Giving all forecasting to one person works less well.
beats.slack: Neither flow is fully predictable. Orders slip, and production hits problems. [[slack]]So build in some slack, and the obvious place is inventory. [[cost]]But inventory costs money to build and to keep. [[low]]Hold it at the lowest-value stage, like raw eggs, not cooked breakfasts. [[flex]]It is cheaper there, and it can still become whatever the customer orders.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where should the slack sit?
beats.staff: The same method runs an office. [[work]]Use your indicators and their trends to forecast the workload ahead. [[peak]]Without a forecast, staffing stays at its highest level, and work expands to fill the time available. [[match]]With one, you can move people to where the work will be. [[std]]It takes standards you believe in, and the discipline to staff by them.
beats.inspect: Now quality. Every flow needs checkpoints: [[c1]]when work comes in, [[c2]]while it is in process, [[c3]]and before it goes out. [[early]]Reject a defect before you invest more in it. There are two ways to check. [[gate]]A gate holds everything until it passes. Safe, but it slows the flow. [[mon]]Monitoring samples a few and keeps the rest moving. A problem may slip through, but for the same money you can check far more. [[rel]]Lean toward monitoring when experience says big problems are unlikely.
beats.waive: Suppose incoming material fails inspection. [[back]]You can send it back, and perhaps stop the line. [[use]]Or you can accept it and live with more rejects later. [[group]]It is usually a question of cost, best decided by a balanced group: quality, production and design together. [[never]]There is one exception. Never pass anything that could fail in the customer's hands. [[pace]]Think of a component inside a pacemaker. If it fails after implant, the cost is far more than money.
beats.variable: Quality is not constant, so your checking should not be either. This is variable inspection. [[new]]When work is new or shaky, look often. [[less]]As it comes back clean, look less. [[prob]]If a problem shows up, [[again]]check more closely until it settles. People rarely do this, mostly out of habit. The same rule tells you how closely to supervise. [[all]]Checking everything is meddling, and people stop owning their work. [[none]]Checking nothing leaves you with surprises.
beats.visa: Grove gives a real case. [[apps]]The American embassy in London handled about a million visa applications a year, and was swamped. [[ok]]About ninety-eight percent were approved. [[all]]Yet every single one was checked in full. [[fix]]Its fixes, like sorting applications into fast and slow lanes, added overhead without adding output. [[sample]]A thorough check on a sample, chosen by set criteria, would have cleared the backlog, [[irs]]much as tax audits keep most returns honest without examining each one.
beats.q3: Quick check. How closely should you look?
beats.leverage: Finally, productivity: output divided by the labor that goes in. [[fast]]You can raise it by doing the same work faster. [[lev]]Or by changing the work so each hour yields more. That is leverage. Automation is one route. Work simplification is another. [[steps]]Write down every step in a process, leaving none out. [[why]]Ask why each one exists. [[cut]]Remove the ones that are there only by habit or formality. [[res]]Grove expected a first pass to cut thirty to fifty percent of steps, and found about thirty percent across office work.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Build to forecast, and have each team own its forecast. [[w2]]Keep slack where the work is worth least. [[w3]]Gate what could hurt the customer. Monitor the rest. [[w4]]Check more when work is new or shaky, less when it is steady. [[w5]]Raise leverage by removing steps, not by rushing. [[end]]Now try the lesson practice.
